notes.text: The Resettlement of Jerusalem. The Chronicler focuses on the worship personnel who return to Jerusalem from exile.

The summarizing conclusion to the tribal genealogies of all Israel in chs. 2–8. Judah’s exile to Babylon for breach of faith (see 2 Chron. 36:14–20) parallels the fate of the northern tribes (“they broke faith”; see 1 Chron. 5:25–26). the Book of the Kings of Israel. See note on 1 Kings 14:19.
Repopulated Jerusalem includes people from Ephraim and Manasseh, as well as Judah and Benjamin. The Judahites are listed as descendants of the patriarch’s sons.
The priests in postexilic Jerusalem are praised for their temple ministry. Their numbers (1,760) have grown significantly (compare 1,192 in Neh. 11:12–14).
Levitical singers and musicians include descendants of Asaph and Jeduthun, choir leaders in David’s day (6:39; 25:1).

The Levitical gatekeepers’ authority is traced to their service under Phinehas (v. 20; see Num. 25:6–11) and their appointment by David (1 Chron. 9:22; 26:1–32). Along with their primary duty of safeguarding the temple, the gatekeepers were also responsible for the utensils and supplies used in the daily sacrifices (9:28–32).
making the flat cakes. God notices and remembers those who faithfully perform routine tasks in service to him.

The Genealogy of Saul. This is repeated from 8:29–38 to introduce the Chronicler’s account of Saul’s reign (ch. 10). While Saul’s dynasty ended with his death (10:6), his family line continued for many generations (9:40–44).
